pending_articles.title: Thrombin cleavage of circulating osteopontin in the lung drives hippocampal neuroinflammation and acute delirium-like neurologic dysfunction after acute kidney injury
pending_articles.content: Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a common clinical problem with high morbidity and mortality due to frequently occurring secondary organ complications, including acute neurologic dysfunction, such as delirium. Specific mechanisms responsible for this kidney-brain crosstalk are unknown but hypothesized to include uremic toxins and neuroinflammation secondary to systemic inflammation. Here we show that uremic mice with AKI show hippocampal monocytic neuroinflammation associated with acute delirium-like neurologic dysfunction only in the presence of circulating osteopontin fragments. Mechanistically, circulating osteopontin (OPN/Spp1) released by the injured kidney was cleaved by thrombin in the lung into OPN-N and OPN-C-terminal fragments. Both OPN fragments were required to drive upregulation of the monocyte chemoattractant chemokine-ligand-2 (CCL2) in hippocampal endothelial cells. AKI mice lacking OPN or unable to activate OPN by thrombin cleavage showed kidney injury and serum uremic toxin elevations like wt controls but were protected from hippocampal CCL2 upregulation, monocyte recruitment, and delirium-like symptoms. Systemic application of an OPN or CCL2 neutralizing antibody was protective. Our results suggest that a specific kidney-released circulating factor, osteopontin, drives acute neurologic dysfunction after AKI and challenge the widely held hypothesis that uremic toxins play a dominant role. They also identify thrombin cleavage of OPN as a potential therapeutic target and critical switch for the remote functions of circulating OPN.

pending_articles.title: Molecular analysis of 55 dopamine transporter variants from psychiatric patients reveals convergent mechanisms of dysfunction
pending_articles.content: Rare genetic variants are increasingly recognized as contributors to neuropsychiatric disease and may reveal underlying pathobiological mechanisms. The dopamine transporter (DAT), encoded by SLC6A3, regulates dopaminergic neurotransmission through rapid dopamine (DA) reuptake. Although disease-associated DAT variants have been linked to disorders ranging from infantile parkinsonism to neuropsychiatric disease, the molecular basis of DAT dysfunction remains poorly understood. Here, we systematically investigated 55 DAT missense variants identified in the iPSYCH2012-nested case-control cohort. By assessing transport activity, inhibitor binding, cell-surface expression, subcellular localization, amphetamine responsiveness and constitutive DA efflux, we resolved the variants into seven phenotypic classes. These reflected distinct molecular defects, including impaired substrate and ion coupling, destabilized intramolecular interactions, and defective folding, trafficking or surface expression. Molecular dynamics simulations provided structural insight into representative variants. Collectively, our findings reveal mechanistic convergence of genetically diverse DAT variants and establish a framework for interpreting the pathogenicity of newly identified SLC6A3 variants.
pending_articles.author: Campana, A., Alves da Silva, L., Degrandmaison, J., Stoier, J. F., Kastner, N., Paggi, L. A., Kooti, F., Klein Herenbrink, C., Newman, A. H., Sitte, H. H., Werge, T., Herborg, F., Stockner, T., Gether, U.

pending_articles.title: Cask dysfunction in inhibitory neurons reveals distinct synaptic and epileptic phenotypes in mouse models of CASK-related disorder
pending_articles.content: Epilepsy is a major neurological manifestation of genetic neurodevelopmental disorders, yet how genetic disruptions produce distinct seizure phenotypes remains poorly understood. CASK-related disorder is an X-linked neurodevelopmental disorder frequently accompanied by epilepsy. It is caused by pathogenic variants in CASK, which encodes calcium/calmodulin-dependent serine protein kinase, a protein with diverse molecular functions. Here, we establish sex-specific mouse models of CASK-related disorder and identify epileptic phenotypes in both sexes. Cell type-specific Cask deletion identifies inhibitory neurons as a critical cellular locus of distinct forms of epileptic activity. Cask deficiency in parvalbumin- or somatostatin-expressing inhibitory neurons primarily causes spike-wave discharges or motor seizures, accompanied by reduced spontaneous or evoked inhibitory synaptic transmission, respectively. Thus, Cask dysfunction in different inhibitory synapses and circuits produces distinct seizure phenotypes. These findings reveal how cell type-specific synaptic dysfunction shapes epilepsy in CASK-related disorder and may provide insights into diverse neurological phenotypes of neurodevelopmental disorders.
pending_articles.author: Jiang, K., Lee, D., Yang, L.-T., Luo, Z., Karatayev, S., Menon, N., Vaidya, B., Medico, S., Xue, M.

pending_articles.title: Modern speech recognition systems exhibit human-like word recognition but superhuman use of statistical dependencies between words
pending_articles.content: Advances in machine learning have yielded machine systems that approach human performance on real-world perception tasks. For speech recognition, it remains unclear whether such models' behavior resembles that of humans. We addressed this question by measuring word recognition abilities in humans and models across 272 speech distortions, providing a detailed behavioral fingerprint. Three recent industry speech recognition models trained on hundreds of years of speech outperformed humans. However, in conditions where linguistic context was removed, they matched human performance well, suggesting that the models are superhuman in their ability to leverage statistical dependencies between words. Experiments manipulating model training data suggest that training data variability and realism contribute to the match to human perception. Overall, the results show that superhuman performance is now possible with systems that are optimized over enough data and suggest that accurate models of human speech recognition require optimization over appropriate tasks and amounts of speech.
pending_articles.author: Magaro, A., Elbanna, G., Shook, E., Kell, A., Saddler, M. R., McDermott, J. H.

pending_articles.title: The global geometry of optimal neural representations
pending_articles.content: Efficient coding hypothesizes that neural activity optimally represents information under resource constraints. The global structures of such optimal population codes are difficult to study theoretically, and previous works have usually resorted to either focusing on local properties like fine discrimination or placing restrictions on the parametric forms of neural tuning. We address the general problem by analytically deriving the neural representation that minimizes the all-pairs average classification error of a one-dimensional circular variable under various forms of neural response noise. Our method is based on formulating the space of neural response distributions as a statistical manifold whose geometry can be simplified through a generalized version of variance-stabilizing transformations. The theory fully characterizes the complete family of optimal population codes and allows us to make two novel predictions. First, an optimal code should allow the existence of oppositely peaked bimodal tuning curves. Second, there should be a correlation between spike count variability and tuning sharpness. We validate both of these predictions in the mouse head direction system.
pending_articles.author: Tian, G. J., Doiron, B.

pending_articles.title: Region-Specific Changes in the Aging Enteric Nervous System
pending_articles.content: As human life expectancy increases, understanding the physiological changes that accompany aging becomes increasingly important. Gastrointestinal (GI) dysfunction is common with age, and age-related changes in the enteric nervous system (ENS), which regulates GI motility, may contribute to this decline in function. Studies of the aging ENS have reported contradicting results, potentially reflecting the substantial regional heterogeneity of the ENS and the fact that most studies focus on only one or two areas of the GI tract. Neurons in the myenteric plexus, which regulate intestinal contractions and motility, are organized into ganglia that form circumferential stripes along the length of the gut. Here, we systematically compare neuronal and glial density and organization across all five regions of the small and large intestine in young (3-4 month-old) and aged (22-26 month-old) mice. We find that neuronal density remains unchanged with age across all regions, despite localized changes in ganglia organization. Although the overall stripe-like arrangement is preserved, ganglia are less aligned with stripes in the duodenum and ileum, while those in the ileum and distal colon are smaller, contain fewer neurons, and have a greater proportion of neurons located outside the ganglia. Glial cell numbers vary regionally with age, increasing in the duodenum and distal colon but decreasing in the proximal colon. The proportion of Calretinin+ neurons, meanwhile, remains stable across the small intestine. Together, these findings reveal that aging is associated with selective, region-specific remodeling of myenteric plexus cytoarchitecture rather than uniform structural decline across the GI tract. This comprehensive regional analysis may help reconcile conflicting reports of age-related changes in the ENS.

pending_articles.title: Natural language processing for suicidal behavior detection in short Spanish clinical notes from first-contact interviews
pending_articles.content: IntroductionSuicide is a multifactorial phenomenon influenced by social, cultural, biological, and psychological factors, whose early detection remains challenging. According to the World Health Organization, suicide is the third leading cause of death among individuals aged 15–29 years, representing a major public health concern for young populations worldwide. In first-contact clinical settings, screening opportunities are often constrained by limited time, sparse patient information, and operational workflows. This study evaluates the feasibility of detecting suicidal behavior from short Spanish-language texts collected during initial screening interviews.MethodsThe dataset comprises 374 anonymized records labeled as “no suicidal behavior,” “ideation,” “planning,” or “attempt,” with a strong imbalance toward “attempt,” reflecting operational clinical usage rather than population-representative sampling. To address data scarcity, we applied data augmentation methods (Easy Data Augmentation for Spanish, backtranslation, and large language model-based synthesis), validated through statistical analysis and clinician-based plausibility assessments.ResultsExploratory analyses revealed highly constrained and overlapping lexical patterns across classes, indicating the challenging nature of the task. A Support Vector Machine achieved 0.53 macro F1 in binary classification (“suicidal behavior” vs. “no behavior”), while BETO, a Spanish BERT model, reached 0.36 macro F1 in multiclass classification. Under the same text-only conditions, human specialists achieved macro F1 scores of 0.29 and 0.15 respectively; however, these results were based on only 20 real texts evaluated with double annotation across five specialists and should therefore be interpreted cautiously.DiscussionAlthough performance is modest compared to studies using full clinical records, these findings suggest that short-text machine learning could support nonspecialists in first-contact settings. Future work should expand datasets and explore multimodal approaches, including voice and text, to improve clinical applicability and early detection.

recently_processed.title: Precision of sensory representations in cortex is indexed by alpha power and pupil dilation, and tracks the dynamics of correlated noise
recently_processed.content: Sensory representations fluctuate in precision from moment to moment, shaping the fidelity of perception and memory. Population-coding theory proposes that these fluctuations are constrained by correlated variability within neural populations, yet linking these mechanisms to behaviour and brain state in humans has remained challenging. Here we combined EEG with an encoding-decoding framework to reconstruct orientation-selective population responses and quantify representational precision dynamically over time. Precision predicted subsequent working-memory performance and evolved in close correspondence with the dynamics of correlated variability between decoded orientation channels. Following stimulus onset, correlated variability was selectively suppressed among similarly tuned channels, the pattern predicted to maximise coding fidelity. Prestimulus alpha power and pupil size independently predicted representational precision, linking these dynamics to endogenous cortical and neuromodulatory state. Together, these findings identify candidate mechanisms and accessible physiological markers of representational precision in humans.
recently_processed.author: Chekroud, S. R., Kolling, N., O'Reilly, J. X.

recently_processed.title: PROGMF: Progressive Multimodal Fusion and Representation Learning for Incomplete Neuroimaging Data
recently_processed.content: Multimodal neuroimaging studies often involve cohorts with partially overlapping data modalities. Many conventional multimodal fusion methods rely on participants with complete observations across the selected modalities. We introduce Progressive Multimodal Fusion (ProgMF), a novel fusion framework for learning multimodal source representations from incomplete neuroimaging data without imputing missing observations. ProgMF integrates modalities sequentially through independent vector analysis (IVA), cross-stage component alignment, and anchor-guided representation transfer, allowing information learned from earlier-stage cohorts to inform subsequent multimodal decompositions. We evaluated ProgMF on four neuroimaging-inspired synthetic modalities, while varying subject overlap, observation noise, modality relatedness, and fusion orders. ProgMF generally achieved lower source-recovery errors than complete-case IVA and the evaluated imputation-based methods, with larger improvements as multimodal subject overlap decreased. We further applied ProgMF to structural MRI gray matter, resting-state functional network connectivity, and 18F-florbetapir (AV45) amyloid positron emission tomography data from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative. ProgMF achieved higher mean cross-modal fusion scores than the imputation-based baselines and a modest improvement over complete-case IVA. Among the 293 participants with complete multimodal observations, two recovered source component vectors showed significant associations with clinical diagnosis across cognitively normal, mild cognitive impairment, and dementia groups. Both sources were also significantly associated with cognitive performance and dementia severity. The recovered sources exhibited diagnosis-related structural and amyloid PET patterns involving regions such as the hippocampi, precuneus, and cingulate cortices. Our findings support progressive representation transfer as an effective approach for recovering coherent, interpretable multimodal sources from participants with incomplete modality coverage.
recently_processed.author: Solomon, V., Calhoun, V. D., Adali, T., Silva, R. F., Angryk, R. A., Liu, J.

recently_processed.title: Counterfactual aging in individual digital twin brains uncovers a latent dimension of resilience to aging
recently_processed.content: Cognitive reserve concerns why the same aging causes less decline in some individuals than others, a question that digital twin brains can address by aging each individual in silico. Here we present Brain-VRNN, a connectome-constrained variational recurrent neural network trained on longitudinal multitask functional MRI. Its regenerated brain signals reproduced four functional aging markers of unseen individuals (r = 0.93-0.96) and identified each person (accuracy 0.98). Without cognitive scores, its global latent learned a trait dimension stable within each person, which helped predict future cognition. Crucially, when every individual underwent the same counterfactual aging, those with a lower trait value declined more, yet recovered up to 1.6 times as much with a reduction in body mass index, a modifiable dementia risk factor. Aging single regions showed that different markers decline through different regions, with a lateral temporal-angular region shared by all. Brain-VRNN brings within-person simulation to cognitive reserve.
recently_processed.author: Takahashi, Y., Idei, H., Tomita, H., Yamashita, Y.

recently_processed.title: Aging remodels the neuronal activity-dependent transcriptome
recently_processed.content: Experience-driven neuronal activity induces coordinated transcriptional programs in neurons and glia that support plasticity and memory. How aging reshapes these activity-regulated gene (ARG) programs, and whether activity mitigates or exacerbates aging phenotypes, remain open questions with implications for cognitive decline. Here, we develop novel-environment and chemogenetic paradigms to characterize age-dependent remodeling of ARG transcriptomes in the mouse hippocampus at single-cell resolution. Aging contracts youthful ARG programs in both gene number and dynamic range, a contraction that persists under controlled chemogenetic stimulation independent of behavior. In parallel, novel experience in older mice reveals a latent transcriptional competence. First, distinct sets of genes respond to neuronal activity selectively in older cells. Second, enhancing activity in older animals partially reverses, or buffers, basal aging-associated changes across the transcriptome. Novel experience counteracts aging-associated changes in the target genes of the memory regulator CREB1 and the ER-stress sensor ATF6 across cell types. These data constitute a resource for neuronal activity-dependent transcription across the lifespan and identify a basis for the benefits of cognitive engagement: novel experience buffers age-related transcriptional drift.
recently_processed.author: Um, J., Lei, H. C., Nakamura, K., Tycksen, E., Adelman, J. W., Pollina, E.

recently_processed.title: New software package: ERPLAB Studio
recently_processed.content:
We are excited to announce the release of a new EEG/ERP analysis package, ERPLAB Studio. We think it’s a huge improvement over the classic EEGLAB user interface. See our cheesy “advertisement” video to get a quick overview.

Rather than operating as an EEGLAB plugin, ERPLAB Studio is a standalone Matlab program that provides a more efficient and user-friendly interface to the most commonly used EEGLAB and ERPLAB routines.

With ERPLAB Studio, you automatically see the EEG or ERP waveforms as soon as you load a file. And as soon as you perform an operation, you see what the new EEG/ERP looks like. For example, when you filter the data, you immediately see the filtered waveforms.

You can even select multiple datasets and apply an operation like artifact detection on all of them in one step. And then you can immediately see the results, such as which EEG epochs have been marked with artifacts.

We give you access to EEGLAB’s ICA-based artifact correction tools, but with a nice bonus. You can plot the ICA activations in the same window with the EEG data, making it easy to see which ICA components correspond to specific artifacts such as eyeblinks.

The program has an EEG tab for processing continuous and epoched EEG data, and an ERP tab for processing averaged ERPs.

The automatic ERP plotting makes it easy for you to view the data laid out according to the electrode locations. And we have an Advanced Waveform Viewer that can make publication-quality plots.

ERPLAB Studio is mainly just a new user interface. Under the hood, we’re running the same EEGLAB and ERPLAB routines you’ve always used. And scripting is identical.

ERPLAB Studio is included in version 11 and higher of ERPLAB. You simply follow our download/installation instructions and then type estudio from the Matlab command line.

If you’re new to ERPLAB, we strongly recommend that you go through our tutorial before starting to process your own data.

If you already know how to use the original version of ERPLAB (which we now call ERPLAB Classic), you can quickly learn how to use ERPLAB Studio with our Transition Guide.

We also have a manual that describes every feature in detail.

recently_processed.title: New Paper: Does the P3b component reflect working memory updating?
recently_processed.content:
Carrasco, C. D., Simmons, A. M., Kiat, J. E., & Luck, S. J. (in press). Enhanced working memory representations for rare events. Psychophysiology. https://doi.org/10.1111/psyp.70038 [preprint]

For decades, many ERP researchers have believed that the P3b wave (sometimes called P300) is a scalp manifestation of a process that updates working memory. This idea originated with Manny Donchin’s context updating hypothesis of the P3b (Donchin, 1981). Donchin’s idea of context was pretty different from working memory, but as this hypothesis percolated through the field over time, it gradually morphed into the idea that the P3b reflects the updating of working memory.

Rolf Verleger mounted a major attack on the original context updating hypothesis in a classic review article in BBS (Verleger, 1988), which was followed by a vigorous rebuttal by Donchin and Coles (1988). These are interesting papers to read, but they did not settle the issue. In the ensuing years, as the field became more focused on working memory instead of context, I’m aware of no studies that directly tested the hypothesis that the P3b reflects working memory updating.

One reason for the lack of direct evidence is that the oddball paradigms typically used to elicit the P3b do not provide a sensitive assessment of working memory. In a typical paradigm, for example, participants would see a sequence of 90% Xs and 10% Os, and the task would be to press one button for X and another button for O. The responses are made immediately, so it is not necessary to store the stimuli in working memory. Even if participants were asked to make a delayed response, the Xs and Os are so easily discriminable that memory performance would likely be at ceiling.

A few years ago, my lab (especially Carlos Carrasco, Aaron Simmons, and John Kiat) got interested in trying to test the working memory encoding hypothesis. We ran a couple of experiments, but we couldn’t quite figure out the right design. Finally, we figured it out. We used a modified oddball paradigm in which a little dot appeared at one of many locations around an circle (see Figure 1).

On each trial, participants pressed one button if the circle was close to one of the four cardinal axes (left, right, top, and bottom) and a different button if it was close to one of the four diagonals (upper left, upper right, lower left, and lower right). One of these two categories was rare (the oddballs) and the other was frequent (the standards; counterbalanced across trial blocks). As is usual in oddball paradigms, the P3b was much larger for trials in the rare category than for trials in the frequent category (see Figure 2).

The main question was whether the location of the dot was encoded in working memory better for the oddball trials than for the standard trials. To assess this, the experimental design contained occasional probe trials on which participants used the mouse to click on the exact location of the dot (see Figure 3). That is, after participants made the cardinal/diagonal buttonpress responses, they were sometimes then asked to click on the remembered location of the dot. This happened on only 12.5% of trials, selected at random, so that participants would mainly focus on the oddball task.

We looked at the accuracy of these probe responses, calculated as the (absolute value of the) angular distance between the true location and the reported location. As shown in Figure 4, the response error of the probe responses was reduced for the oddball trials relative to the standard trials. In other words, working memory was better for the P3b-eliciting oddball trials than for the standards. Moreover, we found that participants with large P3b amplitudes on oddball trials had smaller response errors on oddball trials (whereas this correlation was not present for standards).

At first glance, these findings seem like support for the idea that the P3b reflects working memory updating. However, the story is not that simple. For example, when we looked at single-trial P3b amplitudes, response errors were not lower for trials with larger P3b amplitudes than for trials with smaller P3b amplitudes.

We also used ERP decoding to test whether the exact location of the dot was better stored in working memory on oddball trials than on standard trials (click here for information about how ERP decoding works and how you can decode your own data using ERPLAB Toolbox). As shown in Figure 5, we could decode the location of the dot better on oddball trials than on standard trials during the period following the P3b component. Note, however, that this was a pretty small difference that only barely crossed the threshold for statistical significance (p = .048). I would really like to see this effect replicated before fully believing it. However, the behavioral effect was rock solid (and replicated in a follow-up experiment).

What can we conclude from these findings? When we started the project, I knew that it would be difficult to draw any strong causal conclusions about the relationship between the P3b component and working memory updating. That is, even if we saw both a larger P3b and improved working memory on oddball trials, this would just be a correlation and could potentially be explained by a third variable such as attention. But if we saw a big difference in working memory between oddballs and standards, and if we found that working memory was better on trials with larger P3b amplitudes, this would be at least consistent with the idea that the process that produces the P3b on the scalp is also involved in working memory encoding.

However, although we saw an enormous difference in P3b amplitude between oddball trials and standard trials, we saw only small differences in working memory between oddballs and standards, whether measured via behavioral response errors on probe trials or EEG decoding accuracy. If the process that generates the scalp P3b voltage plays a major role in working memory encoding, then we would have expected a much larger working memory difference between oddballs and standards. Moreover, although we found that participants with larger P3b amplitudes had smaller response errors, we did not find any evidence that working memory was any better on trials with larger P3b amplitudes (even though we looked very hard for such a relationship). The bottom line is that, although I was really hoping we would finally provide some direct evidence for the working memory encoding hypothesis, the results of this study have actually convinced me that the P3b is probably not related to working memory encoding.

What, then, explains the small but statistically significant differences in working memory accuracy between oddballs and standards, along with the subjectwise correlation between P3b amplitude and behavioral response errors? A very plausible explanation is that both the P3b component and working memory encoding are facilitated by increased attention. That is, there are several sources of evidence that rare events trigger increased attention, and this could independently produce a larger P3b and improved working memory.

Of course, this is just one experiment, so I wouldn’t say that the working memory encoding hypothesis is completely dead. But given our new findings and the general lack of direct evidence for the hypothesis, it’s on life support.

If the P3b doesn’t reflect working memory encoding, then what does it reflect? This seems like a significant question: the P3b is huge and is observed across a broad range of experimental paradigms, and it’s reasonable to assume that the underlying process must be important for the brain to devote so many watts of energy to it. In fact, I find it embarrassing that our field has not answered this question in the 60 years since the P3b was first discovered.

My best bet is that the P3b is related to the process of making decisions about actions (where the term actions is broadly construed to include the withholding of responses and mental actions such as counting). This is related to the fact that the amplitude of the P3b is related to the probability of a task-defined category, not the probability of a physical stimulus category. Rolf Verleger has a nice review of the evidence for this idea (Verleger, 2020). But it is still not clear to me why the brain devotes so many watts of energy to creating a large P3b when a rare task-defined category occurs. Verleger notes that several hypotheses about the P3b are compatible with the finding of a larger P3b for oddballs than for standards, but in my view these hypotheses have a hard time explaining the enormous size of the P3b observed for oddballs. This is a longstanding mystery in need of a solution!
